title: Burs, handpieces and sharps at the chairside
audience: Cleaners and dental assistants who handle trays, handpieces and sharps during changeover.
learningOutcomes: Explain why careless handling of sharps is the leading cause of puncture injuries in a dental surgery.
Remove a loose sharp safely without touching it with bare fingers.
Seal and hand over a sharps box for licensed collection under the site plan.

instruction.heading: Where sharps injuries come from
instruction.body: The source names careless handling of sharps, during treatment and afterwards, as the chief reason for puncture injuries at dental chairs. Tight working space and a limited view of the field make things worse. Burs, scalers, scalpels, orthodontic wires and needles all belong to that group, and the risk runs through the whole changeover, not only through the procedure itself.

instruction.heading: Burs and handpieces
instruction.body: A bur is removed from its handpiece before the handpiece leaves the unit, so that a bur does not travel with it. Reusable burs go into a stand, not into a general container. Before changeover begins, the assistant checks that the operator has taken off any burs or orthodontic wires. A cleaner does not remove a bur from a handpiece unless the role and training allow it.

instruction.heading: Hand passing and trays
instruction.body: Blades like scalpels and scalers are never handed directly from one worker to another. They are dropped into a puncture-resistant receptacle straight after use, and they travel to the instrument area inside a lidded box that resists punctures. Disposable sharps go straight into a sanctioned sharps box at the chairside, near the spot where they were used.

instruction.heading: Containers and collection
instruction.body: Sharps containers stand upright, out of children's reach, and are never overfilled. The source asks for sealing at the fill line, or at roughly three-quarters capacity, followed by collection by a licensed waste contractor under local rules. The cleaner hands sealed containers to the person responsible for collection and does not collect or transport them to a disposal site.

instruction.heading: Needles
instruction.body: A needle is not recapped unless the practice uses a recapping device or a single-handed technique designed for that purpose. Bending or snapping a used needle by hand is never acceptable. Disposable needle and syringe combinations go directly into the sharps container.

procedure: Before you start, confirm the chairside sharps container is in place, upright and not overfull.
Confirm with the operator that burs have left their handpieces before changeover begins.
Lift any loose sharp with forceps or a scoop, never with bare fingers.
Place sharps in the lidded transport container, not in an open tray or a bag.
Seal the container at the fill line, or at roughly three-quarters capacity, label it, and move it to secured storage for collection.
Report any sharps injury or near miss immediately, following “Sharps: handling, containers and injury response” and the practice's exposure protocol.

workedExamples.situation: A loose bur is lying on the tray at changeover, and the operator has left the room.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not pick it up by hand. Use forceps or a scoop to put it into the sharps container or the bur stand, then tell the nurse so the operator knows and the item is accounted for.

workedExamples.situation: On a Friday afternoon, a sharps box sits at roughly three-quarters capacity, and the next session is on Monday.
workedExamples.reasoning: Seal and label the container, then place it in secured storage for licensed collection under the site plan. Do not leave it open at the chairside over the weekend.

equipmentAndPpe: Forceps or a scoop for loose sharps
Approved sharps containers that meet the applicable standard
Thick utility gloves for handling the container, and goggles

commonErrors.error: Handing a scalpel directly to someone else.
commonErrors.prevention: Place the sharp in the tray and let the receiver take it from the tray.

commonErrors.error: Overfilling a sharps container so the lid will not close.
Recapping a needle to tidy the tray.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not recap unless a device or technique designed for it is in use.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Gloves reduce contamination of a sharp's outer surface but do not stop a sharp from piercing the glove. Gloves are not a sharps control.
The cleaner's handover of sealed sharps to the person responsible for collection is covered. This lesson does not grant a licence to collect, carry or treat clinical waste.
The source names Australian standards and state rules.

qualityStandard: No sharp is passed hand to hand at any point during changeover.
Every sharps container is sealed at the fill line or at roughly three-quarters capacity, and then labelled.
documentationEvidence: Sharps container change record with the date and location
summary: Careless sharps handling is the most common reason for puncture injuries at dental chairs.
Lift sharps with forceps or a scoop, put them in a box, and never hand them over directly.
Seal containers at the fill line and hand them over for licensed collection.

knowledgeChecks.question: A cleaner finds a loose bur on the tray at changeover. What is the best action?
options: Pick it up with fingers and drop it in the general bin and wipe the tray afterwards.
Use forceps or a scoop, place it in the sharps container or bur stand, and tell the nurse.
Leave it, because it is not the cleaner's job and tell the nurse at the end of the day.
Put it in the general bin and then move on to the next tray without a word.

knowledgeChecks.question: The sharps box sits high in the bin, with its lid close. Which arrangement is safe?
options: Keep it upright, stable and out of children's reach.
Set it on a tray that can tip over near the edge.
Leave the lid off for easier drop-in near the front.
Overfill it so it is used fully and then carry it.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must a scalpel never be handed straight across to someone else?
options: Direct hand-to-hand passing is a common route to a sharps injury, so the sharp goes into a tray instead.
It is quicker, so it is fine and the nurse is busy with the patient and cannot look up.
The scalpel is sterile, so the risk is removed and the hand-off is quicker for the team.
Only gloved hands may pass sharps and the gloves must be new for each hand-off in the room.

sourceReferences: ADA Guidelines for Infection Control, 3rd ed. (Australian Dental Association, 2015), sections B.4 (management of sharps and their disposal), C.5 (burs) and the exposure definitions; rights: user-held; reworded (no copying)
